lessons.title: Search and count: grep, cut, sort, uniq, wc
lessons.goal:
Learn the small tools that answer most log questions: find lines, pick columns, and count.

Why it matters: each tool does one thing. Joined with pipes they answer questions such as "which client sends the most requests?" in one line.

setup.note: Create a small web server log to practise on. The addresses are from the documentation ranges, so they are fake.

steps.title: The data
steps.text: Every line of `web.log` is one request: client address, time, request, status code and bytes. `wc -l` counts lines, `head` and `tail` show the start and the end.

steps.title: grep selects lines
steps.text: `grep PATTERN FILE` prints the lines that match. `-n` shows line numbers, `-c` counts matches, `-v` inverts, `-i` ignores case.

steps.title: Extended regular expressions
steps.text: `grep -E` allows `|` (or), `+`, `?` and groups. Here: all status codes that start with 4 or 5.

steps.title: cut picks columns
steps.text: `cut -d' ' -f1` splits each line at blanks and prints the first field. The result is a list of client addresses.

steps.title: sort, uniq: count the repeats
steps.text: `uniq` only merges **adjacent** equal lines, so you must `sort` first. `uniq -c` adds the count. `sort -rn` sorts numbers, biggest first.
steps.under: `sort` reads all input before it can write (it must see every line to know the order). That is why a pipeline with `sort` shows nothing until the input ends. It uses temporary files if the data does not fit in memory.

steps.title: tr and tee
steps.text: `tr` translates or deletes single characters. `tee` copies its input to a file **and** to the next command, so you can save a middle result.

quiz.explain: Equal lines that are not next to each other are counted separately.

quiz.q: Which command prints the number of lines containing `404`?

options: Sends output to a file and to stdout
quiz.explain: It splits the stream in two.

check.scenario: Print the three most frequent client addresses of web.log with their counts, as one pipeline.
check.answer: `cut -d' ' -f1 web.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3`. Cut the first field, sort so equal lines are adjacent, count with `uniq -c`, sort by count descending, keep three.

lessons.title: sed and awk
lessons.goal:
Learn `sed` for editing a stream and `awk` for working with columns.

Why it matters: when `cut` and `grep` are not enough (substitute text, add up numbers, group by a column) these two tools do it in one line without a script.

setup.note: Create a small web server log to practise on. The addresses are from the documentation ranges, so they are fake.

steps.title: sed substitutes text
steps.text: `sed 's/OLD/NEW/'` replaces the first match on each line. Add `g` for all matches. With `-n` and `p` it prints only the lines you select.

steps.title: sed can delete and edit files in place
steps.text: `sed '/PATTERN/d'` deletes matching lines. `-i.bak` edits the file in place and keeps a backup with the suffix.

run.cmd: cp web.log copy.log; sed -i.bak 's/GET/get/' copy.log; ls copy.log*
grep -c get copy.log; grep -c GET copy.log.bak

steps.title: awk splits every line into fields
steps.text: awk reads a line, splits it into `$1`, `$2`, ... and runs your code. `NF` is the number of fields, `$NF` the last field. The pattern before `{...}` selects the lines.

steps.title: awk can calculate
steps.text: Variables keep values between lines. `END` runs after the last line. Here: total bytes, and the average.

steps.title: awk arrays group by a key
steps.text: An awk array can be indexed by any string. `c[$key]++` counts occurrences. This replaces `sort | uniq -c` and lets you do more with each group.

run.cmd: awk '{c[$(NF-1)]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' web.log | sort
awk '{b[$1] += $NF} END {for (k in b) print k, b[k]}' web.log | sort -k2 -rn | head -n 2

steps.under: awk is a tiny interpreter. It reads input record by record (default separator: newline) and splits each into fields (default separator: blanks). `-F:` changes the field separator, for example for `/etc/passwd`.

quiz.explain: `$NF` is the field whose number is NF, the last one.

quiz.q: Which sed command deletes lines containing `debug`?

options: Edits f in place and saves f.bak
quiz.explain: The suffix after -i is the backup name.

options: Counts lines per value of the first field
quiz.explain: It keeps one counter per distinct key.

check.scenario: Show the total bytes sent to each client of web.log, largest first.
check.answer: `awk '{b[$1] += $NF} END {for (k in b) print k, b[k]}' web.log | sort -k2 -rn`. awk adds the last field per client address; sort orders by the second column, numerically, descending.

lessons.title: find, xargs, diff and safe pipelines
lessons.goal:
Learn to find files by properties, to pass their names safely to other commands, and to compare files.

Why it matters: file names can contain spaces and even newlines. A pipeline that ignores this works on your test data and fails (or deletes the wrong file) in production.

setup.note: Create a small web server log to practise on. The addresses are from the documentation ranges, so they are fake.

steps.title: find walks a directory tree
steps.text: `find DIR TESTS ACTION`. Tests: `-name`, `-type f|d`, `-size`, `-mtime`. The default action prints the path.

steps.title: Run a command on each match
steps.text: `-exec CMD {} \;` runs CMD once per file. `-exec CMD {} +` passes many files to one run, which is much faster.

steps.title: xargs builds a command line from input
steps.text: `xargs CMD` reads words from stdin and runs CMD with them as arguments. It is the bridge between a list and a command that takes arguments.

run.cmd: echo a b c | xargs -n1 echo item
run.output:
item a
item b
item c

steps.title: The trap: file names with spaces
steps.text: `xargs` splits at blanks. A file name with a space becomes two arguments, and the command acts on the wrong names.

run.output:
wc: my: No such file or directory
wc: notes.txt: No such file or directory
3 other.txt
3 total

steps.title: The fix: NUL-separated names
steps.text: A file name can never contain a NUL byte. `find -print0` ends each name with NUL and `xargs -0` reads that format.
steps.under: `xargs` also splits the work: if the argument list would exceed the kernel limit for `execve` arguments (`getconf ARG_MAX`), it runs the command several times.

steps.title: diff shows what changed
steps.text: `diff -u OLD NEW` prints a unified diff: lines starting with `-` were removed, `+` were added. The exit code is 0 if the files are equal, 1 if they differ.

steps.title: patch applies a diff
steps.text: A diff is a patch. `patch` applies it to the old file and produces the new one.

run.cmd: cp v1.txt v3.txt; patch v3.txt < change.patch

quiz.q: A file is called `my notes.txt`. What goes wrong with `ls | xargs rm`?
Which pair is safe for any file name?
quiz.explain: NUL cannot appear in a path.

quiz.q: What is the exit code of `diff a b` when the files differ?
What is the difference between `-exec ... \;` and `-exec ... +`?
options: `+` passes many files per command run

check.scenario: You must delete all `*.tmp` files older than 7 days under /var/app, including names with spaces. Write the command.
check.answer: `find /var/app -type f -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7 -print0 | xargs -0 rm --` or simply `find /var/app -type f -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7 -delete`. First run it with `-print` to see the list.

interview.q: How do you find the top 5 IP addresses in an access log?
interview.a: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5`. See [the lesson](#/lesson/5/grep-sort-count).

interview.q: What is the difference between grep, sed and awk?
interview.a: grep selects lines, sed edits a stream with commands such as substitute and delete, awk is a small language that splits lines into fields and can compute. See [sed and awk](#/lesson/5/sed-awk).

interview.q: Why must the input of uniq be sorted?
How do you safely pass file names with spaces from find to another command?
interview.a: `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 CMD`, or `find ... -exec CMD {} +`. See [find and xargs](#/lesson/5/find-xargs-diff).

interview.q: How do you replace text in many files in place?
interview.a: `sed -i 's/old/new/g' files` (add `.bak` to keep backups). Test without -i first. Combine with `find -exec` or `xargs -0` for trees.

interview.q: What do the exit codes of grep mean?
interview.a: 0: a line matched. 1: no line matched. 2: an error occurred. Scripts often test this: `if grep -q pattern file; then ...`.

glossary.def: A pattern language for matching text. grep -E uses extended regular expressions.
A column of a line after splitting at a separator. awk names them $1, $2, ...
Commands joined by | so that each one's output is the next one's input.
A zero byte used between file names because it cannot occur in a name (find -print0).
The patch format printed by diff -u with - and + lines.

commands.desc: Show matching lines with line numbers.
Search a tree with an extended regex.
Copy stdin to FILE and stdout.
Edit in place with a backup.
Print the first and last field.

commands.desc: Show differences as a unified diff.
